content.text:
The current ownership contract lives in [`docs/architecture/client-boundaries.md`](docs/architecture/client-boundaries.md), with file-level type destinations in [`docs/architecture/type-ownership.md`](docs/architecture/type-ownership.md). `AGENTS.md` summarizes that layout for agents; it is not the full inventory.

## What the report currently owns

The report is layered. The **current architecture contract** (plus the application-state follow-up) is the live rule. The later phase sections are historical snapshots from TIDY-477.

Ownership is by **folder role**, not by product app:

| Folder | Owns |
|---|---|
| `schema/` | Resource definitions, cross-layer product identity, billing/account wire contracts, legacy persistence encodings |
| `client/datafn/` | Client storage and sync runtime; generic resource errors and read-only lookup |
| `client/runtime/` | Browser infrastructure: account transport, network authority, connectivity, logging, native embed, inference, browser audio |
| `client/features/` | Capability implementations (`calendar`, `collections`, `focus`, `memory`, `spaces`, `system`) |
| `client/products/` | Product composition (Nucleum, Memotron, Pointron, etc.) |
| `client/config/` | Client product identity and declarative navigation metadata |
| `client/elements/` | UI primitives, keyboard/interaction-mode contracts, reusable modal chrome, portable Markdown display |
| `client/components/` | Shared charts, nested lists, time selector, record grid/star/trash, shortcut listener |
| `client/application/` | Account/settings, library rendering, modals, commands, subscription, host wiring |
| `client/stores/` | Shared reactive state and permanent shell contracts |
| `client/layout/` | Navigation, tabs, sidebar, product menu, application shells |
| `client/actions/` | Generic DOM actions only |
| `services/account/` | AuthFn, DataFn, SearchFn, generated mappings |
| `shared/` | Cross-layer utilities (for example WAV serialization) |
| `apps/` | Deployable product bundles and Playwright harnesses |

Capability-specific ownership inside features is explicit: **memory** owns Markdown editing, tags, word-count, and PDF-overlay actions; **spaces** owns combinations; **focus** owns scheduled notifications and session/goal/task state.

Shared stores are split the same way. `app.store.ts` keeps product state. Account session stays in `account.store.ts`. Deletion confirmation lives in `client/application/account/account-deletion.ts`. Subscription lives in `client/application/subscription/`. File upload/signing lives in `client/stores/files/`. Overlays, resource actions, panels, and recents live under `client/stores/`. Navigation and menu persistence live under `client/layout/`.

The import rules match that map: features cannot import product or application implementations; shared components cannot import features/products/application; DataFn and runtime cannot import UI, features, or application composition. Outside a capability, callers must use a path listed in `tools/check/feature-entrypoints.json`.

File-level type ownership is a separate catalog: [`docs/architecture/type-ownership-inventory.json`](docs/architecture/type-ownership-inventory.json) records 383 type modules and their destinations. `node tools/check/type-ownership.mjs` and `npm run check:architecture` enforce that.

## Is this represented in `AGENTS.md`?

**Partially, at folder/rule level. Not as a file-by-file map.**

Root [`AGENTS.md`](AGENTS.md) (Tidigit Constitution v1.2.1) does encode the same organization:

- The onboarding layout lists the same top-level folders and their roles (`client/features`, `client/datafn`, `client/application`, `client/layout`, `client/runtime`, `client/config`, `client/stores`, `services/account`, `schema`, `shared`, `apps`).
- The **Ownership and composition** section states the same split: app state in `app.store.ts`, navigation in `client/layout/navigation`, commands in `client/application/commands`, account session must not own deletion/files/subscription, generic actions in `client/actions`, and so on.
- It tells agents that `client-boundaries.md` and `type-ownership.md` are **authoritative**, and that historical validation records are snapshots only.
- The Sync Impact Report in that file is the changelog for this: it says v1.2.1 “clarified current application, layout, runtime, config, store, and capability ownership after the client migration.”

What `AGENTS.md` does **not** contain:

- The complete type-module inventory
- The public feature entry-point list
- Per-file destinations after each TIDY-477 move
- The historical phase-by-phase verification record

[`conduct/AGENTS.md`](conduct/AGENTS.md) is unrelated. It only describes Conduct spec folders (`conduct/features`, `conduct/changes`), not product-code ownership.

So: folder ownership is represented in `AGENTS.md` as agent rules. File and type ownership are represented in the architecture report, the JSON inventory, and the checkers. If those ever diverge, the report’s current-contract sections win.

content.text:
`client/components` is reusable presentation. `client/application` is product composition. Command Bar is composition, so it belongs in application.

## The split

**`client/components`** (`@nucleum/components`) holds widgets that stay useful without knowing which product is running: charts, nested lists, TimeSelector, maps, file view, generic record thumbnails, a shortcut listener. They take data and callbacks. They do **not** import features, products, or application. Architecture enforcement rejects both direct and transitive imports of those layers.

**`client/application`** (`@nucleum/application`) is the shell that wires capabilities into a running app: command execution, account/settings, library, subscription, modal orchestration, resource hosts. It **is** allowed to import features, products, components, layout, and stores. Application depends on components; the reverse is forbidden.

That is the same rule as the overlay/thumbnail moves: reusable chrome went to components or elements; the thing that decides *what* to open, *which* capability owns it, and *how* to navigate stayed in application.

## Why Command Bar is application

Command Bar is not a search input with a results list. It is the product command palette.

1. **It runs the product action registry.** `CommandBar.svelte` and `CmdResults.svelte` call `requireCommandHost().resolveAction` / `runAction`. That host is installed from `resource-hosts.ts` as `configureCommandHost(actionRunner)`. `actionRunner` lives in `client/application/commands` and reads `$appStore.actions`, hide-by-embed/OS/account, navigation, and overlay presentation.

2. **It maps commands onto feature and product screens.** `commandBar/actionMap.ts` imports Calendar, CreateCollection, memory linking, Pointron clocks, Memotron search, subscription, settings, help, and debug. That file is the definition of application composition. Putting it under `components` would immediately fail:

```242:245:tools/check/architecture.mjs
    /^client\/(components|elements)\//.test(from) &&
    /^client\/(features|products|application)\//.test(to)
```

3. **It is the command UI the contract names.** `client-boundaries.md` says application owns “command UI.” `AGENTS.md` says command execution belongs in `client/application/commands`, with shared callers using the host configured by the application shell.

4. **The reusable pieces already live below it.** Buttons, empty states, shortcut text, markdown rendering, and keyboard toolbar come from `client/elements`. Matching/listening for shortcuts lives in `client/stores/keyboard` and `client/components/keyboard`. Command Bar sits above those primitives and decides which command to run.

A close parallel is `ComponentShortcutListener.svelte`: it lives in components because it only listens and uses `ShortcutHost`. The runner, default keymap, and command palette stay in application. Same pattern as thumbnails: `ResourceThumbnailBase` is a component; the menus and navigation host are supplied by the owner.

If Command Bar moved to `components`, either the architecture check would fail, or you would have to strip out action execution, `actionMap`, product/feature imports, and `appStore.actions`. What remained would be a generic search popover, which is not what Command Bar is.

Those four lines in `resource-hosts.ts` are leftover sibling imports. In `client/application` they are not a common pattern.

## Why the warning fires

`tidigit/alias-imports` is **warn-only** and only flags **parent** relatives (`../…`), plus `$lib`, `client/`, `apps/`, `shared/`, `schema/`. Same-folder `./foo` is allowed.

```140:148:tools/alias-utils.mjs
export const DISALLOWED_IMPORT_PATTERNS = [
  /^\.\.{1,2}\//, // relative traversals
  /^client\//,
  /^apps\//,
  /^shared\//,
  /^schema\//,
  /^\$lib\//,
  /^\$lib$/
];
```

ESLint also only runs on `ts`/`js`. Svelte files are not checked, which is why most remaining `../` in layout/features never show up as this warning.

The intended replacements for this file are already in `tools/alias-map.json` as `@nucleum/application`:

- `../commands/action-runner` → `@nucleum/application/commands/action-runner`
- `../shortcuts/shortcuts.config` → `@nucleum/application/shortcuts/shortcuts.config`
- `../record/resource-link.utils` → `@nucleum/application/record/resource-link.utils`
- `../record/Records.svelte` → `@nucleum/application/record/Records.svelte`

They are same-package siblings. Someone wired the hosts with local relatives; the alias rule still wants the workspace path so ownership stays visible.

## How common this is

Workspace aliases already dominate. Across 2,755 source files / ~15k import specifiers:

| Pattern | Imports | Files |
|---|---:|---:|
| `@nucleum/` / `@21n/` aliases | 10,044 | 1,412 |
| same-dir `./` (allowed) | 1,695 | 424 |
| parent `../` (restricted) | 968 | 275 |
| `$lib` leftovers | 135 | 73 |

Most of the 968 `../` hits are **not** client UI: `ios` 439, `apps` 205, `deployment` 178, `server` 74. Those areas often sit outside the alias map.

Inside **`client/`** there are only **41 parent-relative imports in 24 files**. In **`client/application`**, `resource-hosts.ts` is the only one:

```
client/application/composition/resource-hosts.ts   (4 imports)
client/features/*                                  (10 files, mostly Svelte)
client/layout/*                                    (8 files, all Svelte)
client/elements/*                                  (4 files, all Svelte)
client/persistence/dexie/dexie.indexing.worker.ts  (1)
```

The other client leftovers are typical intra-package hops: `../collection.store`, `../Icon.svelte`, `../topNav/tabs/tabs.store`. There are also 24 remaining `$lib/...` imports in 9 client files, mostly older memory capture/node UI.

So this is not a house style in application. It is a thin leftover from the incremental alias migration (`specs/001-to-incrementally-replace`), which converted ~10k specifiers, left the ESLint rule at warn, never linted Svelte, and never treated `npm run lint` as a repo-wide ESLint gate. `resource-hosts.ts` is one of the few TypeScript files where Cursor still surfaces it.

content.text:
**Keep intra-package `../`. Only require aliases when the import leaves the workspace package. Ignore the `$lib` leftovers until you touch those files.**

## Intra-package `../` vs aliases

`../collection.store` should stay relative.

That store is private. It is not in `feature-entrypoints.json` or `@nucleum/features` exports. The architecture contract already says internal capability callers use relative paths to private modules, so Node and the checker reject outsiders.

Turning those hops into `@nucleum/features/collections/collection.store` would make a private module look public, without changing who can legally import it. Same-package `./` is already allowed; `../` inside the same capability is the same idea one folder up.

Require aliases only when the import **crosses a workspace root** in `tools/alias-map.json`:

- `client/application` → `client/features` must be `@nucleum/features/...`, and only through a declared public entry
- `client/features/memory` → `client/elements` must be `@21n/elements/...`
- `$lib/client/...`, `client/...`, `apps/...` must never come back

The current ESLint rule is broader than that: it flags every `../`, including private intra-capability hops. That is why it fights the ownership contract. If you change one thing in tooling later, narrow the rule to “`../` that escapes the current alias root,” and leave Svelte intra-package hops alone.

`resource-hosts.ts` is the exception worth aliasing locally. Those targets are already public `@nucleum/application/*` exports, not private capability modules. Aliasing them quiets the warning you have open and does not fake a public API.

## `$lib` leftovers

Do not make them the next project.

They are the actually-wrong pattern: `$lib/client/elements/Icon.svelte` is a SvelteKit path into another package and should be `@21n/elements/Icon.svelte`. There are only about five memory files. Mechanical, no UI change.

Still, ignore them until those files are touched.

- They sit in Capture / node settings UI. A dedicated sweep is a drive-by on a capability you are not working in.
- Most are Svelte, so ESLint never sees them anyway.
- `NodeSettings.svelte` already mixes `$lib` and `@21n/elements` in the same script. Convert the rest when someone is already in that file.

If a TS file like `webCapture.service.ts` is opened for real work, replace `$lib/client/utils/account.utils` with `@21n/utils/account.utils` in that same change. Do not schedule a memory `$lib` cleanup on its own.

**Practical rule:** aliases at package boundaries, relatives inside a package, `$lib` only when you are already editing the file. For today, that means the four `resource-hosts.ts` imports and nothing else.

Do not schedule a memory $lib cleanup on its own.

Why not?

A dedicated `$lib` sweep is leftover style, not a bug. It does not earn its own change.

Those five memory files still resolve through SvelteKit. `$lib/client/elements/Icon.svelte` works today. Replacing it with `@21n/elements/Icon.svelte` does not change Capture, node settings, or upload behavior. The original alias migration already treated leftovers like this as opportunistic backlog and left the lint rule at warn.

It also would not fix the warning you have open. Most of the leftovers are Svelte, and `tidigit/alias-imports` does not run on Svelte. A memory cleanup would not make `resource-hosts.ts` cleaner or the alias policy clearer.

The cost is in the wrong place. Those imports sit in Capture and node settings, which are user-visible memory surfaces. The architecture record already has Capture-related Playwright failures as baseline. A “just imports” PR still needs product context, a Capture/settings smoke, and review noise, for a change nobody can see. The constitution also tells agents not to take user-facing files unless that is the job.

`NodeSettings.svelte` already mixes `$lib` and `@21n/elements` in the same script. That is the right grain: convert the rest when someone is already in that file and can check the screen. `webCapture.service.ts` is the one TypeScript leftover; fix it if that file is opened for real work.

Scheduling it as its own task turns a three-line habit into a capability touch. That is why I said ignore until touched, not “never fix.”

I'll read the account store against `application/account` and the ownership contract so the placement is from the code, not just the folder name.

`account.store.ts` is session state. `application/account` is account workflow. Features, layout, and elements can read the first; they cannot import the second.

## Why the store is not in `application/account`

The store holds “who is signed in”: `dataMode`, token, `userInfo`, plan snapshot, sign-in/sign-out, AuthFn session hydrate. Login screens, OAuth start, and deletion confirmation live next door in `client/application/account/`.

That split is intentional. Memory capture, markdown, layout (`BaseLayer`, `AuthGuard`, top nav), elements (`OfflineStatusMessage`), maps, extensions, and products all import `@nucleum/stores/account.store`. If that file moved under `application/account`, those callers would import application composition.

That is forbidden:

- Features cannot import application
- Shared components and elements cannot import application
- `@nucleum/stores` does not depend on `@nucleum/application` or `@nucleum/features`

The checker also keeps the store thin. These methods are retired from `account.store.ts` and must not come back: `delete`, `confirmDelete`, upload helpers, subscription/payment. Deletion is `account-deletion.ts`. Billing is `application/subscription`. Uploads are `stores/files`.

So `application/account` *uses* the store. It does not own it.

## Why `client/stores/` exists at all

It is the shared reactive layer: current app facts and host contracts that many packages read, without pulling in product UI.

| Layer | Holds |
|---|---|
| `client/runtime` | Transport: AuthFn client, connectivity, embed, logging. No Svelte UI state. |
| `client/stores` | Shared session, preferences, overlays, uiState, files, keyboard matching, resource selection, command host. Hosts are configured by the shell. |
| `client/application` | User workflows: login, settings, command bar, library, deletion, subscription. |
| `client/features` | Capability implementations: memory, focus, collections. |
| `client/layout` | Chrome: nav, tabs, layers. |

`AGENTS.md` says the same thing: stores hold shared reactive state and permanent shell contracts; domain workflows belong with their owner.

That is why overlays, shortcuts, and recents moved *into* stores: features and layout need them, and those modules must not import application. Application wires the hosts in `resource-hosts.ts`. Stores stay below that line.

`account.store` is the account version of that pattern. Session is a shell fact. “Delete my account” is an application workflow.

I'll trace the elements → account.store edge and compare `stores/` to the old catch-all `types/` so the naming concern is grounded in the actual split.

`elements` barely depends on `account.store`. One feedback chip does, and that is a leftover, not the point of the directory.

## Why that import exists

The only elements file that imports the account store is `OfflineStatusMessage.svelte`. It reads `$account.dataMode` to choose “Offline” vs “Data warning”, then calls `requireCommandHost().runAction(Action.OFFLINE_STATUS)`.

Layout and settings mount it as a small badge. It lives in `elements/feedback` because it looks like a primitive. It behaves like shell chrome: it knows session mode and a product command. A true primitive would take `dataMode` / `isOffline` as props and let the parent decide. That would drop the account import.

So this is not “elements depends on account.” It is one widget reaching into shared session instead of being given the fact it needs. Same smell as other elements that pull `appStore`, `fileUpload`, or `recentsStore` (cover picker, tables). Those are also shell-aware controls sitting in the primitives package.

`@21n/elements` lists `@nucleum/stores` as a peer because many primitives read view, appearance, context, overlays, and hosts. Account is not a special case; it is the thinnest of those edges.

## `stores/` is not the old `types/`

Your instinct about the **name** is right. The **job** is different.

`client/types` and `shared/types` were retired because they had no owner. Anything could land there, then get re-exported. The replacement rule was: put the type next to the implementation.

`client/stores` is a **dependency layer**, not a dump. Features, layout, and elements may import it. It must not import application, features, or products (except through hosts the shell installs). That rule is why session, overlays, shortcut matching, and recents live there instead of under `application/`.

Domain state is already colocated when it has a real owner:

- Focus session → `client/features/focus/session.store.ts`
- Collection store → `client/features/collections/collection.store.ts` (private, relative)
- Tabs → `client/layout/topNav/tabs/`
- Account deletion → `client/application/account/account-deletion.ts`

What remains in `client/stores` is shared shell state: who is signed in, viewport, appearance, overlay host, command host, generic UI persistence, file upload, resource selection. The architecture doc already says this leftover set is **not certified as universally minimal**.

The confusing part is the label. `stores/` names the Svelte mechanism, the way `types/` named the TypeScript mechanism. Mentally it is closer to “shared shell state and host contracts” than “all state.”

I would not rename or explode the folder. That would be another catch-all shuffle. Further splits only pay off when a concrete consumer benefit appears, which is why overlays and keyboard already moved as named sub-owners instead of “more stuff in stores.”

**Practical read:** keep `account.store` in `client/stores` because layout, features, and elements need session without importing application. Do not treat `stores/` as the place all new state goes. If a store has one capability owner, colocate it there. The OfflineStatusMessage account import is optional coupling, not proof that primitives own session.
